# Transfer learning earns a test, not a default

Transfer learning is worth testing on your ~998 Specim IQ leaf cubes, but the literature does not show it beating well-tuned classical spectroscopy models, and for leaf-level plant disease nobody has run the decisive experiment. The best-supported gain comes from ImageNet-pretrained 2D CNNs with a learned 204-to-3 channel adaptor. In a small-data regime (1,000 training images) that approach beat training from scratch by about 13 accuracy points on EuroSAT (88.4 vs 75.2) ([Perez & Maji, ar5iv](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2108.01555)). That evidence comes from satellite imagery, not leaves, and a from-scratch model there is a data-hungry image network, not a tuned SVM. Hyperspectral foundation models (SpectralGPT, HyperSIGMA, HyperFree, SpectralEarth, DOFA) were pretrained on 30 m to 1 m remote-sensing pixels. None has been tested on leaf disease, and on the one close-range benchmark the in-domain model beat the frozen foundation model at 10% and 25% data ([HS3-Bench, arXiv 2604.26478](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.26478)). Published grapevine red blotch (GRBV) and leafroll (GLRaV) accuracy is modest (80-87% binary at leaf level, 62-77% four-class) and comes from image-level random splits. The one in-domain study that held out data properly saw accuracy fall 10-65 points ([Nguyen 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7866105)). My recommendation is to build the grouped-validation harness and a tuned classical baseline first, then add pixel-level spectral deep models, then test one ImageNet-adaptor model and one wavelength-aware foundation model against that bar. Treat everything beyond the baseline as a hypothesis, because most evidence below is adjacent-domain.

## Published grapevine numbers are modest and probably optimistic

The closest prior work is Sawyer et al. (2023). It used 496 detached-leaf images from 248 vines, a 40-band Senop camera at 510-710 nm, and PCR-confirmed labels ([PMC10036814](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036814/)). Random forest (RF) on the mean spectrum reached 79.5% binary accuracy over the entire dataset. A 3D-CNN on the full cube reached 80.9%, and 82.4% vs 87.0% on symptomatic leaves. In the four-class task the two were 62.2% and 67.0%, and RF was actually better on pre-symptomatic leaves (77.7% vs 76.9%). GRBV was the weak class: 35% (RF) and 49% (CNN) overall, and in the symptomatic subset (only 22 images) 8% vs 57%. Reported pre-symptomatic binary accuracy of 82.8-85.6% shows the spectra carry signal before visible symptoms. The same paper reports human visual assessment of RGB images at only about 50% binary.

Two caveats limit how far these numbers transfer. First, validation was stratified 5-fold CV at image level, with two leaves imaged per vine and no vine grouping described, so same-vine leaves can sit on both sides of a split. Second, the CNN saw the whole cube while RF saw only the mean spectrum, so the 1-5 point CNN edge mixes architecture with input information. Field and aerial studies sit lower or similar: 73.3% for canopy imaging with 23 bands and 87.0% for UAV GRBV (ASEV abstracts seen only as search summaries, and I could not verify their validation schemes) ([ASEV field](https://asev.org/abstract/grapevine-virus-detection-using-field-hyperspectral-images-and-machine-learning-models), [ASEV UAV](https://asev.org/abstract/scalable-vine-level-assessment-grapevine-red-blotch-virus-infections-aerial-hyperspectral)). Airborne AVIRIS-NG GLRaV-3 reached 85-87% with RF on pixels using 70/30 plus 10-fold CV ([bioRxiv](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.10.04.510827v1.full)). No retrieved GRBV/GLRaV-3 paper uses Specim IQ, held-out vineyards, or reports AUC.

The only in-domain measurement of how much split choice matters is Nguyen et al. (2021) on grapevine virus (GVCV) with a Specim IQ: pixel-level RF cross-validation gave 89.7-95.3% while testing on held-out images gave 28.7-77.8%, below chance on two dates ([PMC7866105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7866105)). Remote-sensing work shows the same mechanism: a 3D-CNN dropped from 96.17% to 55.20% when train/test patch overlap was removed (a 2026 non-peer-reviewed preprint) ([arXiv 2610.08770 summary](https://deeplearn.org/arxiv/841523/data-leakage-in-patch-based-hyperspectral-image-classification:-quantifying-the-impact-of-spatial-overlap)). Informative wavelengths cluster in the visible and red edge (586-596 nm pre-symptomatic; about 530, 600, 650 and 700 nm symptomatic) with NIR contributing in some studies ([Sawyer 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036814/), [Nguyen 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7866105)). Your 400-1000 nm range covers all of these, a wider window than Sawyer's 510-710 nm, but it lacks the SWIR water bands used in airborne work.

## Classical spectroscopy is the bar, and deep learning has not clearly cleared it

The one fully matched comparison on a small leaf set is tobacco disease (95 leaves, 462 bands, pixel spectra sampled after a leaf-level split). Test accuracy ran Transformer 99.35%, ANN 98.93%, SVM 97.90%, XGBoost 97.50%, PLS-DA 88.47%, RF 82.67% ([PMC12816246](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12816246/)). A tuned SVM, gradient-boosted model or small neural net on pixel spectra is therefore the realistic bar, while PLS-DA and RF are cheap sanity checks and not the bar. Differences of 1-2 points on a ~95-leaf test set are noise, and absolute numbers will not transfer to your ~1000 leaves and harder viral task. Stem-rust work found linear SVM, logistic regression and LightGBM on first-derivative spectra gave F1 0.94-0.96, with per-band standardization giving the largest single gain ([PMC12608451](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608451/)). In Nguyen's Specim IQ study, deep image-level features plus RF reached only 50% on held-out images while pixel-level PCA plus RF reached 73.6%. The wheat co-infection study (EfficientNet-B0, 81% overall) is often cited as evidence for deep learning, but it reported no classical baseline ([PMC12595906](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12595906/)).

Preprocessing has no consistent winner. Savitzky-Golay (SG) smoothing, first derivatives and per-band standardization are the safest defaults. Band selection (SPA, CARS) hurt SVM and PLS-DA in the tobacco data but not the ANN, so it should be treated as a per-model hyperparameter chosen inside the CV loop ([PMC12816246](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12816246/)). Pixel spectra from one leaf are near-duplicates, so the leaf must be the split and inference unit. The tobacco study split at leaf level before sampling pixels, and a sensible pipeline then caps pixels per leaf and averages pixel probabilities back to the leaf. Evidence for attention-based multiple-instance learning (MIL) on leaf hyperspectral data is essentially absent (one soybean MIL paper was seen by author list only), so it is an untested refinement. For your two binary labels, binary relevance (one classifier per disease) is the natural baseline. The one co-infection paper used mutually exclusive combination classes, and rare combinations were poorly classified (39 and 36 samples) ([PMC12595906](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12595906/)). The choice between binary relevance, label powerset and classifier chains is my judgment, with no plant-specific evidence behind it.

## ImageNet transfer has the best-supported upside, foundation models the weakest

Perez & Maji tested ways to feed multichannel data to ImageNet-pretrained VGG and ResNet models. Their conclusion was that simple linear projection to 3 channels or band-subset selection is usually most effective, while inflating first-layer filters to N channels was worst or near-worst ([arXiv 2108.01555](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.01555), [tables](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2108.01555)). With 1,000 training samples, VGG-D with a linear adaptor scored 88.4% on EuroSAT-small vs 75.2% from scratch, and 54.9% vs 27.2% on LEGUS-small. The gap shrank at full size (97.1 vs 95.7). A multi-view adaptor (several parallel 3-channel views fused by pooling) added more (94.4 on EuroSAT-small) and plateaued near 5 views. PCA initialisation did not help, and a 10x adaptor learning rate gave gains of 3.7-5.8% on average. Using all bands beat RGB conversion (70.3 vs 97.7 on EuroSAT). These are single fixed splits on non-leaf data, so they support the mechanism, not a leaf-disease outcome. The counter-evidence is Lee et al. 2019, where an HSI-pretrained CNN fine-tuned no better than one trained from scratch for shallow networks ([arXiv 1901.08658](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08658)), and the same is plausible for a ~1000-sample task. Note that your 204 bands are strongly collinear and your cubes are small (~150 px), so a 1x1 adaptor is a lightweight, plausible fit, but whether it beats a scratch spectral model here is exactly what is unknown. The closest unreleased precedent is a proximal-sensing masked autoencoder (MAE) that included Specim IQ data, where an ImageNet ViT-L beat it on two of three tasks (e.g. F1 97.98 vs 93.18 on DriedFoods) ([arXiv 2503.01628](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.01628v1)), and a close-range segmentation benchmark where an RGB-pretrained DINOv2 with an HSI adapter reached 76.58 mIoU vs 60.60 for the remote-sensing HSI foundation model ([arXiv 2604.26478](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.26478)). Both point to RGB-pretrained backbones as at least competitive with remote-sensing hyperspectral ones.

Among hyperspectral foundation models, public weights are verified for DOFA (MIT licence, any channel count given wavelengths in micrometres), Copernicus-FM (CC-BY-4.0), HyperSIGMA (Apache-2.0 code, weight licence unstated) and SpectralEarth (licence unstated) ([DOFA](https://github.com/zhu-xlab/DOFA), [Copernicus-FM](https://github.com/zhu-xlab/Copernicus-FM), [HyperSIGMA](https://github.com/WHU-Sigma/HyperSIGMA), [SpectralEarth](https://github.com/AABNassim/spectral_earth)). SpectralGPT expects 12 Sentinel-2 bands, so a 204-band cube would need PCA that destroys wavelength correspondence ([arXiv 2505.15334](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.15334v1)). HyperSIGMA re-initialises its patch embedding if band counts differ ([arXiv 2406.11519](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.11519v2)). HyperFree's weight release is unconfirmed ([arXiv 2503.21841](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.21841v1)). Reported foundation-model gains on small labelled sets are 1-3 points over specialised baselines (HyperFree 93.39 vs 92.65 OA; HyperSL +3 mIoU in-domain) and no paper applies any of them to leaf disease. Pretraining on Indian Pines, Pavia or Salinas is not a serious option: each is a single scene, and the literature pairs sensors with similar resolution and spectral range ([Remote Sens. 13(5):930](https://www.doi.org/10.3390/RS13050930)), which a 30 m scene is not to a leaf cube. Self-supervised pretraining on your own cubes is plausible but unproven at this scale; the MAE evidence uses tens of thousands of tiles ([TerraMAE, arXiv 2508.07020](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.07020v1)).

## Validation decides whether any result is believable

Group at the highest independent unit available. That means vine first, then cut-out leaf, with pixels never crossing the split, and then variety and imaging session as stress tests. Your four varieties are the main unmeasured hazard. If infection status correlates with variety, vineyard or imaging day, a model can learn those instead of disease. No retrieved GRBV/GLRaV paper tested this, and Sawyer's authors themselves flag cultivar as a possible unintended cue ([PMC10036814](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036814/)). The diagnostic is cheap: train a variety-only (and session-only, if known) predictor, check it against label balance per variety, and compare leave-one-variety-out accuracy with grouped random-split accuracy. The size of the grouped-vs-image-split gap on leaf data is unmeasured in the literature I have, so the Nguyen and remote-sensing numbers above are warnings, not estimates for your data. Beyond that, the protocol I recommend (from the notes, partly my own judgment): nested, repeated, grouped CV with all scalers, SPA/CARS and PCA fit inside training folds only ([Guo et al. 2017, snippet](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlepdf/2017/ay/c7ay01363a)); leaf-level metrics only; macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall and AUC with bootstrap CIs over groups; a permutation test; class weights rather than pixel-count balancing; and, for the two labels, folds stratified on the label combination. Report the majority-class and variety-only predictors next to every model. Finally, compare models on identical folds, since 1-2 point gaps are within noise at these sample sizes.

## Top 5 approaches to implement and test, in order

1. **Leaf-grouped classical baseline with the full validation harness (do first).** Build the nested, repeated, vine/leaf-grouped CV and leave-one-variety-out stress test, then fit RBF-SVM, L2 logistic regression and XGBoost/LightGBM on leaf-mean and pixel spectra, with PLS-DA and RF as sanity checks. Grid {white/dark reflectance calibration, SG smoothing, SG first derivative, SNV, per-band standardization fit on train} x {all bands, SPA/CARS}, and use binary relevance for the two labels. Reasoning: this is the bar every deep model must clear, it is the cheapest experiment, and it exposes variety confounding before any deep model can exploit it. Evidence: SVM/XGBoost/ANN within about 1-2 points of a transformer and well ahead of PLS-DA/RF in tobacco ([PMC12816246](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12816246/)); linear SVM/LR/LightGBM on derivatives gave F1 0.94-0.96 in stem rust ([PMC12608451](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608451/)); pixel-level classical beat deep image-level features on held-out Specim IQ data ([Nguyen 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7866105)).

2. **Pixel-level spectral deep model from scratch with leaf-level aggregation.** Train a small ANN or 1D CNN on pixel spectra (cap pixels per leaf, spectral augmentation such as intensity scaling and small band-wise noise), average probabilities per leaf, and optionally try attention-MIL pooling. Reasoning: it multiplies the training signal without needing pretrained weights, matches how the best small-set models were built, and is the natural from-scratch counterpart for judging transfer. Evidence: ANN was the best non-transformer model at 98.93% in tobacco ([PMC12816246](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12816246/)); relighting augmentation helped a pixel CNN at every training-set size (snippet only, [arXiv 1611.09007](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.09007)); a 1D CNN beat PLS-DA on grapevine esca (no numbers retrieved). MIL itself has no verified plant evidence, so test it as a variant, not an assumption.

3. **ImageNet-pretrained ResNet with a learned 204-to-3 adaptor versus a from-scratch 2D/3D CNN, same folds.** Use a learned 1x1 convolution (optionally a 3-5 view multi-view adaptor) in front of a ResNet-18/50, with the adaptor at about 10x the backbone learning rate, geometric plus spectral augmentation, and per-cube input. Include a band-subset adaptor and a PCA-3 variant as cheap controls, and skip filter inflation. Reasoning: this is the only transfer-learning option with measured large gains in the 1,000-sample regime, and it is also the direct "transfer vs scratch" answer to your question. Evidence: 88.4 vs 75.2 and 54.9 vs 27.2 for small-data EuroSAT and LEGUS ([Perez & Maji](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2108.01555)); an ImageNet ViT-L beat an HSI-pretrained model on two of three proximal tasks ([arXiv 2503.01628](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.01628v1)). The risk is that the gain vanishes against option 1 or 2, which is a valid result.

4. **Wavelength-aware foundation-model probe with DOFA, frozen then parameter-efficient fine-tuned.** Feed 204 bands with their centre wavelengths, run a linear probe and then LoRA/last-blocks fine-tuning, and run a DINOv2-with-adapter variant alongside it. Reasoning: DOFA is the only verified-public model that accepts arbitrary bands without discarding pretraining, so it is a clean single experiment; the RGB-foundation-with-adapter variant addresses the strongest close-range signal. Evidence: wavelength-conditioned embeddings are documented ([DOFA](https://github.com/zhu-xlab/DOFA)); on close-range data the remote-sensing HSI foundation model gained about +3 mIoU in-domain but lost to in-domain training at 10-25% data, while DINOv2 plus adapter reached 76.58 vs 60.60 ([arXiv 2604.26478](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.26478)). Ranked fourth because no leaf-disease evidence exists and the domain gap (30 m mixed pixels, SWIR-heavy pretraining) is large.

5. **Self-supervised spectral pretraining on your own cubes, then fine-tune.** Use masked-band or masked-pixel autoencoding on all ~998 cubes (labels unused during pretraining; fit inside each training fold to avoid leakage), then fine-tune the pixel model from option 2. Reasoning: it is cheap and adapts to your sensor and illumination exactly, but it is the least supported because the data is highly correlated and small. Evidence: masked-autoencoder gains exist only at the scale of about 22,000 tiles, with a frozen-encoder gain from 76.09 to 83.82 on land cover ([TerraMAE](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.07020v1)); there is no small-leaf-dataset evidence, so expect a null result as often as a gain.

## Deprioritized options

SpectralGPT and HyperSIGMA are deprioritized because they need 12 bands or a re-initialised embedding, which discards the pretraining that justifies them. HyperFree and the 2025 proximal MAE are deprioritized because weight availability is unconfirmed or absent. SpectralEarth and Copernicus-FM are deprioritized because they were pretrained on 30 m EnMAP or multispectral Sentinel data with no leaf-scale results; revisit them only if DOFA shows a signal. Pretraining on Indian Pines, Pavia or Salinas is out because the sources are single scenes in a different spectral and spatial regime. A heavy 3D-CNN or ViT from scratch is out as an early step because Sawyer's CNN advantage came with a different input and a leaky split, and 3D CNNs lost badly on held-out Specim IQ data. First-layer filter inflation is out because it was the weakest adaptor in the only controlled comparison. GAN/diffusion augmentation (one 2025 preprint seen as a snippet) and PLS-DA or RF as the headline baseline are also set aside; the latter two stay as sanity checks.

## Conclusion

The question is not whether transfer learning is worthwhile in the abstract but whether any pretrained representation beats a tuned SVM or pixel-level ANN once leakage is removed. Three things change the framing: the strongest published numbers rest on image-level splits, the strongest transfer gains come from non-leaf data and a weak from-scratch comparator, and the closest close-range evidence favours RGB-pretrained backbones over remote-sensing hyperspectral ones. So the experimental order matters more than any single model: the grouped harness and variety-confound diagnostics come first, and transfer is evaluated against what that harness shows the classical baseline can do.

The largest open risks are specific to your data. Variety or session may be confounded with infection status, GRBV (the minority and hardest class in Sawyer's data) may stay hard, and with ~1000 leaves differences of a few points will sit inside bootstrap noise. Plan for the possibility that classical models or the pixel ANN win, which would still be a publishable finding given how little leaf-level grouped evidence exists. Several cited sources here were seen only as search summaries (ASEV abstracts, Bendel 2020, several baselines), and all numbers from them should be checked against the papers before use.
